newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Strong pound to bloat UK trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Strong pound to bloat UK trade deficit.

text.p: Britain's current account deficit has remained surprisingly resilient in recent months, resisting the expected adverse effect of sterling's strength.
But analysts say the strong pound -- which has appreciated by 16 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August -- will soon start to take its toll on Britain's trade gap.
"As domestic demand in the UK gathers momentum, it is inevitable that the underlying trade position will deteriorate," says Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.

In his first quarter economic review, Jeffrey said the appreciation of the pound, if it continues, would have a more marked slowing effect on export growth than it would on bringing down import prices -- forcing the trade deficit to puff out later this year and next.
In its initial stages, a currency rally exerts downward pressure on import prices and upward pressure on export prices, leading to a narrowing of the trade gap.
This appeared to be the case in December, when the trade deficit with the rest of the world narrowed to 845 million pounds from more than one billion in November.
But that initial slimming -- seen in Britain in the last eight months -- will soon start to peter out, analysts say.
The risk is that a sharp turnaround in supply and demand will bloat the deficit quite dramatically in coming months.
Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets in London, says he expects the deficit to widen to 8.0 billion sterling in 1997 from just 1.5 billion in 1996 -- reducing GDP growth by around 0.75 percent.
But even with sterling's dramatic rally filtering through, the deterioration of the trade deficit will be nowhere near as painful as the levels seen in the late 1980s.
At the high point of the late 1980s economic boom, Britain's trade deficit peaked at a searing 22.0 billion sterling -- around 4.5 percent of GDP.
Economists say a quarterly rise of around 2.0 percent, or 2.75 billion stg, constitutes a "pain barrier" above which Britain's current account would present serious hurdles to economic growth.
But for those fearful of a return to the boom-bust economy of the late 1980s and early 1990s, a moderate worsening of the trade gap is a welcome prospect.

Combined with the dampening effect of the pound's strength on core prices and its drag on the recovery in industry, a wider trade gap would help take the heat out of inflation, slowing growth and reducing the need for any substantial tightening of monetary policy.
"The worsening of the trade deficit itself will not be enough to prevent interest rate rises," said Loynes.
"But it could contribute to a slowdown in growth in the second half of this year, which means that rates will not have to go up as far as the markets are currently expecting."

Short sterling interest rate futures, which reflect financial markets' views on the direction of short term borrowing costs in the future, are factoring in official rates above 6.75 percent by the end of this year.
The Bank of England left official rates unchanged at 6.0 percent at Wednesday's monetary meeting.
If the cycle comes around as expected, any concerns about a return to a boom-bust scenario can be laid to rest, according to recent research from the London Business School.

The LBS said it expected GDP growth to rise to 3.3 percent in 1997, but then slow to 2.7 percent in 1998 and 2.3 percent the year after, while manufacturing growth would lag overall growth in 1997 and then pick up in later years.
But it noted possible barriers to this "soft landing" scenario.

"One possibility is that a new Labour government applies the brakes to the economy much harder than we envisage, with the aim of clearly establishing credibility for controlling inflation and reducing the risk the inflationary pressures will build up over the course of the term of government," it said.
